Among My believing servants are those who ask Me for a door of worship, and I know that if I gave it to him, vanity would enter him and corrupt him. Among My believing servants are those whom only wealth sets right, and if I made him poor, poverty would corrupt him. Among My believing servants are those whom only poverty sets right, and if I made him wealthy, wealth would corrupt him. Indeed I manage My servants, knowing what is in their hearts, for I am All-Knowing, All-Aware."

Then Anas said: "O Allah, I am among Your believing servants whom only wealth sets right, so do not make me poor by Your mercy."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verse 28:

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Mujahid, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Thabbat, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yunzilu" (He sends down) with a light (mukhaffafah) pronunciation. The rest read it with the doubled letter (mushaddadah). Ibn Thabbat also, and al-A'mash and others, read "qanatu" (they despaired) with a kasra on the nun. All of this has already been discussed [see vol. 1, pp. 36, 67, and vol. 14, p. 34].

Al-ghayth is the rain. The rain is called ghayth because it gives relief (yughithu) to creation. It is said: "ghatha al-ghaythu al-ard," meaning it reached the land; and "ghatha Allahu al-bilad yughithuha ghaythan," meaning God gave the lands rain; and "ghithat al-ardu tughathu ghaythan," so the land is "ardun maghitha" and "maghiythah" (a land that has been rained upon).

From al-Asma'i, who said: I passed by some of the tribes of the Arabs who had been rained upon, and I asked an old woman among them, "Has the rain come to you?" She said: "Ghithna ma shi'na ghaythan," meaning, "We were rained upon as much as we wished."

Dhu al-Rummah said: "May God fight (qatala) the slave-girl of the sons of so-and-so, how eloquent she is! I asked her, 'How was the rain among you?' and she said, 'Ghithna ma shi'na.'" The first report was cited by al-Tha'labi and the second by al-Jawhari.

Sometimes the cloud and the vegetation are also called ghayth.

Al-qunut means despair (al-iyas). This was said by Qatadah and others. Qatadah said: It is related that a man said to Umar ibn al-Khattab, "O Commander of the Faithful, the rain has failed, the rain has become scarce, and the people have despaired?" He said, "You have been rained upon, God willing," and then he recited: "And He it is who sends down the rain after they had despaired" (﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي يُنَزِّلُ الْغَيْثَ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا قَنَطُوا﴾).

Al-ghayth is that which is beneficial at its time, whereas al-matar (rain) may be beneficial or harmful, both at its time and at other times, said al-Mawardi.

"And He spreads His mercy" (﴿وَيَنْشُرُ رَحْمَتَهُ﴾): it was said to mean the rain, and this is the view of al-Suddi. It was also said to mean the sun appearing after the rain, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the withholding of rain from the people of Makkah for seven years, until they despaired; then God sent down the rain.

It was also said: It was revealed concerning the Bedouin who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the rain on Friday, in the report about seeking rain (istisqa'), as mentioned by al-Qushayri. And God knows best.

"And He is the Protecting Friend, the Praiseworthy" (﴿وَهُوَ الْوَلِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ﴾): "al-Waliyy" is the One who helps His friends (awliya'ihi). "Al-Hamid" is the One praised in every tongue.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning, His signs that indicate His power. "And what He has dispersed in them of living creatures (dabbah)." Mujahid said: this includes the angels and the people, and Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [an-Nahl: 8].[[Verse 8 of Surat an-Nahl.]] Al-Farra' said: He meant what is dispersed in the earth and not in the heaven, like His saying: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [ar-Rahman: 22][[See vol. 17, p. 163.]], and indeed they emerge from the salt water and not the fresh. Abu 'Ali said: its estimated meaning is "and what He has dispersed in one of them," so the genitive (mudaf) was omitted. His saying, "from them," means from one of them. "And He is, over their gathering" meaning on the Day of Resurrection, "when He wills, All-Powerful."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verses 32–33:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among His signs are the ships running in the sea like mountains.﴾ That is: and among His signs, which indicate His power, are the ships sailing in the sea, which, because of their greatness, are as if they were mountains. Al-a'lam (the mountains). The singular of al-jawari is jariyah (ship). Allah the Exalted says: "Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship" [al-Haqqah: 11]. It is called jariyah because it runs (tajri) on the water. Al-jariyah also means a young woman, and she is so called because the water of youth runs in her. Mujahid said: al-a'lam are the palaces, its singular being 'alam, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Al-Mawardi mentioned from him that they are the mountains. Al-Khalil said: everything elevated among the Arabs is an 'alam. al-Khansa' said, mourning her brother Sakhr:

"Indeed Sakhr, the guided ones take guidance by him, / as if he were a beacon (alam) with a fire at its top."

"If He wills, He calms the winds" — thus did the people of Madinah read "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural. "So they remain motionless upon its back" — that is, the ships remain still on the surface of the sea and do not run. Rakada al-ma' rukudan: it became still. Likewise the wind, the ship, and the sun when it stands at midday. Everything that remains in one place is rakid. Rakada al-mizan: it became balanced. Rakada al-qawm: they calmed down. Al-marakid: the places where a person or others rest.

Qatadah read "fa-yazlalna" with a kasrah on the first lam, considering it a dialect form, like dalaltu adillu. He read the lam with a fatha, which is the well-known dialect. "Indeed in that are signs" — that is, indications and evidences "for every patient, grateful one" — that is, patient in trials and grateful for blessings. Qutrub said: an excellent servant is the patient and grateful one, who, when given, gives thanks, and when tested, is patient. Awn ibn Abd Allah said: how many a person bestowed upon is not grateful, and how many a person tested is not patient.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verse 34–35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or He causes them to be destroyed for what they have earned﴾. That is: and if He wills, He makes the winds into violent storms, so that He destroys the ships, meaning He drowns them for the sins of their people. It was also said: "He destroys the people of the ships." ﴿And pardons much﴾ of them, so that He does not drown them along with it; this is related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: ﴿And pardons much﴾ means He overlooks many of the sins, so that Allah saves them from destruction. Al-Qushayri said: the widely known reading is ﴿wa-ya'fu﴾ with a jazm (jussive), and there is a difficulty in it, because the meaning is: if He wills, He calms the wind, so those ships remain motionless, and He destroys them for the sins of their people. So it is not fitting to coordinate ﴿ya'fu﴾ with this, because it becomes [[In H: because it would be "if He wills, He pardons."]] the meaning: "if He wills, He pardons." That is not the meaning; rather the meaning is informing about pardon without the condition of will. Thus it is a coordination with the jussive in terms of wording, not in terms of meaning. Some people read ﴿wa-ya'fu﴾ with a raf' (nominative), and this is good in meaning. ﴿And that those who dispute concerning Our verses may know that they will have no place of escape﴾, meaning the disbelievers: that is, when they reach the middle of the sea and the winds overwhelm them from every place, or the ships remain motionless, they know that there is no refuge for them other than Allah, and no repeller for them if Allah wills their destruction, so they devote worship sincerely to Him. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wa-ya'lama﴾ with raf', the rest with nasb. The raf' is on the basis of a new sentence after the condition and the answer, like His saying in Surah at-Tawbah: ﴿and He will disgrace them and give you victory over them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 14], then He said: ﴿and Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills﴾ [at-Tawbah: 15], with raf'. Its parallel in speech: "If you come to me, I will come to you, and 'Abdullah goes off." Or it is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject. The nasb is on the basis of sarf (diversion), like His exalted saying: ﴿And that Allah may know those of you who strive and may know the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142], it was diverted from the state of jazm to nasb for lightness, disliking the succession of jussives, like the saying of al-Nabighah:

"If Abu Qabus dies, there will die the spring of the people and the sacred month."

[[Abu Qabus is his kunya; he is al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir. He means that he was like the spring in fertility for those who sought him, and like the sacred month for his neighbour, i.e. no one who sought his protection could be reached. "And there remains after him, clinging to the tail-end of a life, whose back is cut and which has no hump."

[[Dhanab of everything: its end and rear. Ajabb al-zahr: one whose hump is cut off. He says: if he dies, we remain at the tail of a life whose front, main part and best have passed, and only its tail remains.]]

This is the meaning of the saying of al-Farra', who said: "If ﴿wa-ya'lama﴾ were jussive, it would be permissible." Al-Zajjaj said: it is put in the nasb by implying "an" (that), because before it there is a jussive; you say: "What you do, I do the like of it, and I honour you." And if you wish, you say: "and I honour you" with jazm. In some copies of the Qur'an it is "wa-li-ya'lama". This indicates that the nasb carries the meaning of "and so that he may know" or "so that he may know". Abu 'Ali and al-Mubarrad said: the nasb is by implying "an", on the basis that the first is taken as in the sense of a verbal noun, i.e. "and there will be from him pardon and that he knows." When he treated it as a noun, he implied "an", as you say: "If you come to me and give me, I will honour you," so you put "tu'tini" in the nasb, meaning: if there is from you a coming and that you give me. The meaning of ﴿min mahis﴾ is: from escape and flight; Qutrub said this. As-Suddi said: from a refuge, and it is derived from their saying: "the camel kicked with it a kick" when it threw it off. From this is their saying: "So-and-so swerves (yahis) from the truth", meaning he turns away from it.

"Then it is [but] enjoyment," i.e., it is only a passing enjoyment in a few days that come to an end and go away, so one should not boast about it. The address is to the polytheists. "And what is with Allah is better and more lasting." He means: the reward for obedience ﴿for those who have believed﴾, who affirmed and declared Allah's oneness, ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾. It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq when he spent all his wealth in obedience to Allah, and the people blamed him. And it has come in a hadith that he spent eighty thousand.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verse 37:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins (al-kaba'ir) and the indecencies﴾. Alladhina (those who) is in the genitive position, conjoined to His saying: "What is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe." That is, it is for those who avoid "the major sins of wrongdoing (kaba'ira al-ithm)." The discussion of the major sins has already passed in "al-Nisa'" [[Verse 31, vol. 5, p. 158 and following.]]. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "kaba'ira al-ithm" in the singular (kabira al-ithm), and the singular may be intended as a plural when it is in construct form, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [[Verse 34, Surat Ibrahim; and verse 18, Surat al-Nahl.]] [al-Nahl: 18], and as occurs in the hadith: "Iraq has withheld its dirham and its qafiz." The rest read it in the plural here and in "al-Najm" [[Verse 32]]. "And the indecencies (al-fawahish)": al-Suddi said: it means fornication (al-zina). Ibn Abbas also said this, and said: "the major sin (kabir al-ithm) is shirk." Some people said: "the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm) are those that the minor sins are forgiven for when they are avoided." The indecencies are included among the major sins, but they are more indecent and more heinous, like killing in relation to wounding, and fornication in relation to solicitation. It was also said: the indecencies and the major sins have one meaning, and the repetition is for the variation of wording, meaning they avoid the acts of disobedience because they are major and indecent. Muqatil said: the indecencies are the acts that necessitate the prescribed punishments (hudud).

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾. That is, they overlook and show forbearance toward those who wrong them. It was said: it was revealed concerning Umar when he was insulted in Makkah. It was also said: concerning Abu Bakr when people blamed him for spending all his wealth, and when he was insulted and he showed forbearance. It is related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Abu Bakr once accumulated wealth, so he gave all of it in charity in the path of good. The Muslims blamed him and the disbelievers faulted him, and then it was revealed: "So whatever you are given of things is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and upon their Lord they rely—up to His saying—and when they are angered, they forgive." Ibn Abbas said: a man among the polytheists insulted Abu Bakr, and he did not respond to him at all, so the verse was revealed. This is among the noble qualities of character: they show compassion toward their wrongdoer and pardon those who act ignorantly toward them, seeking thereby the reward and pardon of Allah, exalted is He, in accordance with His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿And those who restrain their anger and pardon people﴾ [[Verse 134, see vol. 4, p. 206]] [Al 'Imran: 134]. It means that a man insults you and you suppress your anger toward him. Some of them recited:

Indeed I have pardoned my oppressor's wrong to me...
and I have granted it to him, while knowing.

He continued to wrong me, and I pitied him...
until I wept for him because of the wrong.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 42, verse 38:

There are three issues concerning this verse. The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who have responded to their Lord and established prayer﴾. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: They are the Ansar in Medina, who responded to faith in the Messenger when he sent to them twelve chiefs (nuqaba', sing. naqib, "representative") from among them before the Hijra. "And established prayer" means they performed it at its appointed times, with its conditions and its proper forms.

The second is His saying, exalted is He: "and their affair is by consultation among themselves" (shura, consultation). That is, they consult one another about matters. Shura is a verbal noun of shawartuhu (I consulted him), like al-Bushra and al-Dhikra and the like. The Ansar, before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ to them, whenever they wanted to do something, would consult about it and then act upon it, so God praised them for it. This was said by al-Naqqash. Al-Hasan said: meaning that, in submitting to counsel in their affairs, they were in agreement and did not dispute, so they were praised for the unity of their word. Al-Hasan said: No people ever consulted together but they were guided to the most right of their affairs. Al-Dahhak said: it refers to their consultation when they heard of the emergence of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the chiefs came to them until their opinion converged at the house of Abu Ayyub upon belief in him and support for him. It was also said that it refers to their consulting about whatever befell them, so that none of them would keep a piece of news to himself apart from the others. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Consultation is a bond of unity for the community, a test of minds, and a means to what is correct, and no people consult together but they are guided. The wise man has said:

When opinion reaches the point of needing counsel, seek help
from the opinion of an intelligent man or the counsel of a prudent one.

And do not let consultation be a burden upon you,
for the secondary feathers (khawafi) are a strength to the primary feathers (qawadim).[[The two verses are by Bashshar ibn Burd. The khawafi are the feathers which become hidden when the bird folds its wings; the qawadim are the ten feathers at the front of the wing, the largest feathers.]]

Thus God praised consultation in affairs by praising the people who used to act upon it. The Prophet ﷺ used to consult his companions about opinions relating to the interests of wars, and such opinions are many. He did not consult them about the rulings, because these were revealed by God on all their categories: obligatory, recommended, disliked, permissible and forbidden. As for the Companions after God had made that exclusive to Himself (by the end of revelation), they consulted one another about rulings and derived them from the Book and the Sunnah. The first matter the Companions consulted about was the caliphate, for the Prophet ﷺ had not designated anyone for it, until what occurred between Abu Bakr and the Ansar, whose explanation has already passed.[[See vol. 4, p. 224.]] ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "We are content for our worldly affairs with the one whom the Messenger of God ﷺ was content with for our religion." They consulted about the apostates, and Abu Bakr's opinion settled on fighting. They consulted about the grandfather and his inheritance, and about the punishment for wine and its number. After the Messenger of God ﷺ they consulted about wars, to the point that ʿUmar consulted al-Hurmuzan when he came to him as a Muslim concerning the campaigns. Al-Hurmuzan said to him: "The likeness of it, and of those in it from the enemies of the Muslims, is the likeness of a bird which has feathers, two wings and two legs. If one wing is broken, the two legs rise with the other wing and the head; and if the other wing is broken, the two legs and the head rise; and if the head is crushed, the two legs and the two wings go. The head is Kisra, one wing is Caesar and the other is Persia, so order the Muslims to march against Kisra..." and he mentioned the hadith. Some of the wise said: "I have never erred! Whenever a matter distresses me, I consult my people and do what they see. If I am right, they are the ones who are right, and if I err, they are the ones who erred."

The third issue: What the consultation contains of rulings has already passed in Al ʿImran, at His saying: "and consult them in the matter" (Al ʿImran 3:159). Counsel is a blessing. Al-mashura and al-mashura (with a damma on the shin) are both synonyms of al-shura. You say: shawartuhu fi al-amr and istashartuhu with the same meaning. Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When your rulers are your best, your wealthy are your generous, and your affairs are by consultation among you, then the surface of the earth is better for you than its belly; but when your rulers are your worst, your wealthy are your stingy, and your affairs are in the hands of your women, then the belly of the earth is better for you than its surface." He said: it is a gharib hadith. ﴿From what We have provided them they spend﴾: that is, from what We have given them they give in charity. This has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.[[See vol. 1, p. 178 and following.]]

There are eleven issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny (al-baghy) afflicts them﴾, meaning when the polytheists' oppression afflicts them. Ibn 'Abbas said: The polytheists oppressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions, harmed them, and drove them out of Makkah. So God permitted them to leave, established them in the land, and gave them victory over those who oppressed them. This is His saying in Surat al-Hajj: "Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged, and surely God is able to give them victory. [They are] those who were expelled..." [al-Hajj: 39–40] and the rest of the verses. It has also been said that the verse is general, applying to the oppression of every oppressor, whether unbeliever or other. That is, when injustice from an unjust person befalls them, they do not submit to his injustice. This points to commanding good, forbidding evil, and enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud). Ibn al-'Arabi said: God mentioned retaliation against oppression in a context of praise, and He mentioned pardon for a wrong in another place, also in a context of praise. It is possible that one of them abrogates the other. It is also possible that this refers to two situations: first, when the oppressor openly commits immorality, is shameless before the public, and harms the young and the old, in which case retaliation against him is better. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said in a similar vein: "They disliked that they should humiliate themselves, so that the wicked would become bold against them."

The second issue: when it is a slip, or it occurs from one who acknowledges his fault and asks forgiveness, then pardon here is better. In this sense God revealed: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], His saying: ﴿Whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], and His saying: ﴿Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that God should forgive you?﴾ [al-Nur: 22]. I say: This is good. Likewise Ilkiya al-Tabari mentioned in his Ahkam: His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾, its apparent meaning indicates that retaliation in this place is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to God, the Glorified and Exalted, and establishing the prayer? This is to be understood in light of what Ibrahim al-Nakha'i mentioned: they disliked that the believers should humiliate themselves, so that the wicked would become bold against them. This applies to one who transgresses and persists in that. The situation in which pardon is commanded is when the offender is remorseful and has ceased. He also said right after this verse: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, against such there is no way [of blame]﴾. This implies permission of retaliation, not a command to it. He followed it with: ﴿But whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the matters requiring resolve﴾. This is to be understood as forgiving one who does not persist. As for one who persists in transgression and injustice, the better course is retaliation against him, based on the indication of the preceding verse. It has also been said: that is, when tyranny afflicts them, they support one another against it until they remove it from them and repel it. Ibn Bahr said this. It returns to the generality we have mentioned.

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. The scholars said: God made the believers two kinds. One kind pardons the wrongdoer, so He began by mentioning them in His saying, ﴿And when they are angry, they forgive﴾ [al-Shura: 37]. The other kind retaliates against their wrongdoer. Then He clarified the limit of retaliation with His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, so one retaliates against the one who wronged him without transgressing. Muqatil and Hisham ibn Hujayr said: This refers to the one who has been wounded taking retribution (qisas) from the one who wounded him, and not from anything else such as abuse or insult. This was also said by al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and Sufyan. Sufyan said: Ibn Shubrumah used to say: "There is no one in Makkah like Hisham." Al-Shafi'i interpreted this verse as meaning that a person may take from the property of one who betrayed him an amount equal to what that person betrayed him with, without his knowledge. He cited in support the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Hind, the wife of Abu Sufyan: "Take from his property what suffices you and your child." So he permitted her to take that without his permission. The discussion of this has already been fully covered in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 335]. Ibn Abi Najih said: It is to be understood as reciprocity in wounds, and if someone says "may God disgrace him" or "may God curse him," then he may say the same. But slander is not met with slander, nor lying with lying. Al-Suddi said: God only praised the one who defends himself against one who wronged him, without transgression, by not exceeding the measure of what was done to him, as the Arabs used to do. The recompense is called an "evil" because it corresponds to it: the first evil harmed in property or body, and this retaliation harms the other in the same way. All of this has been fully covered in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 335].

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever leaves retaliation and makes peace between himself and the wrongdoer through pardon, ﴿his reward is with God﴾, meaning God will reward him for that. Muqatil said: So pardon is among the righteous deeds. What is sufficient on this has already been covered in Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 207], and praise be to God. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz mentioned on the authority of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: "Which of you are the people of virtue?" Some people will stand up, and it will be said: "Go to Paradise." The angels will meet them and say: "Where to?" They will say: "To Paradise." They will say: "Before the reckoning?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Who are you?" They will say: "The people of virtue." They will say: "What was your virtue?" They will say: "When we were treated with ignorance, we showed forbearance, when we were wronged, we were patient, and when we were harmed, we pardoned." They will say: "Enter Paradise, how excellent is the reward of the workers." He mentioned the hadith. ﴿Surely He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the one who begins with injustice, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has also been said: He does not love one who exceeds the limit in retaliation and goes beyond the bound, as said by Ibn 'Isa.

The fifth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾. That is, if a Muslim defends himself against an unbeliever, there is no way to blame him; rather he is praised for that with respect to the unbeliever. And there is no blame if an oppressor [in one text: the wronged one defends himself; in another: an oppressor defends himself against a Muslim] against a Muslim. So retaliation against an unbeliever is obligatory, against a Muslim it is permissible, and pardon is recommended.

The sixth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, against such there is no way [of blame]﴾. This is evidence that one may exact that right by himself. This divides into three categories. The first: if it is retaliation for a bodily harm owed to a human being, there is no sin upon him if he exacts it without transgression and his right is established before the judges. However, the ruler should rebuke him for having taken the retaliation outside of legal process, because of the boldness it entails in shedding blood. If his right is not established before the judge, then there is no sin on him between himself and God, but outwardly he is to be claimed against and held accountable and punished for his act. The second category: it is a right of God the Exalted in which no human has a claim, such as the punishment for fornication or the amputation for theft. If this is not established before a judge, he is to be taken to account and punished for it. If it is established before a judge, one considers: if it is amputation for theft, the punishment is dropped because the limb to be amputated no longer exists, and no further right is owed for this, since discretionary punishment (ta'zir) is merely disciplinary. If it is flogging, the punishment is not dropped by his act, because he transgressed while the place of punishment remained, so he is subject to its ruling. The third category: it is a right concerning property. The owner may contend for his right until he reaches it, if he is one who knows of it. If he does not know of it, one considers: if he is able to reach it when claiming, he may not take it secretly. If he cannot reach it by claiming, because the one who owes it denies it and there is no evidence to support him, then regarding the permissibility of taking it secretly there are two opinions. One: it is permitted, which is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Two: it is forbidden, which is the view of Abu Hanifah.

The seventh issue concerns His saying, ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾. That is, by their transgression against them, according to the majority of scholars. Ibn Jurayj said: that is, they wrong them by polytheism which opposes their religion.

"And they seek to cause corruption in the earth without right." This means in lives and wealth, according to the majority. Muqatil said: their transgression is their doing of sins. Abu Malik said: it is what the disbelievers of Quraysh hoped, that a religion other than Islam would prevail in Makkah. On this basis, Ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated by jihad, and this applies to the polytheists specifically. Qatadah's view is that it is general, and the apparent meaning of the statement supports this. We have explained this, praise be to Allah.

The seventh point: Ibn al-'Arabi said: this verse corresponds to the earlier verse in Bara'ah, which is His saying ﴿There is no path [of blame] against the doers of good﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91]. Just as Allah negated the path against those who do good, so He affirmed it against those who wrong, and He completed the explanation of both categories.

The eighth point: Our scholars differed regarding a ruler who imposes a fixed sum on the people of a city, collecting it from them and having them pay it according to their wealth. Is it permissible for one who is able to escape this to do so, while in that case the rest of the people of the city are taken for the full amount imposed on them? It was said: no, and this is the view of Sahnun from our scholars. It was said: yes, he may do so if he is able to escape, and this is the view of Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Nasr al-Dawudi, then the Maliki. He said: what supports this is Malik's statement concerning the collector who takes a sheep from the flock of one of the partners when the flock as a whole does not reach the minimum: it is an injustice upon the one from whom it was taken, and he has no recourse against his partners for anything. He said: I do not adopt what is narrated from Sahnun, because injustice has no parallel, and no one is obliged to thrust himself into injustice for fear that the injustice will be multiplied upon others. Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿The path is only against those who wrong the people﴾.

The ninth point: The scholars differed regarding halalah (granting release/forgiveness of debt or wrong). Ibn al-Musayyib would not grant release to anyone regarding honour or property. Sulayman ibn Yasar and Muhammad ibn Sirin would grant release regarding both honour and property. Malik held that release is permitted regarding property but not regarding honour. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, when he was asked about the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, "I do not grant release to anyone," that he said: "That differs." I said to him: "O Abu 'Abd Allah, a man lends to another man and he perishes with no means of repayment?" He said: "I think he should release him, and that is better in my view, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 18]." It was said to him: "A man wrongs a man?" He said: "I do not think that. In my view it contradicts the first. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿The path is only against those who wrong the people﴾, and He, exalted is He, says: ﴿There is no path against the doers of good﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91]. So I do not think he should make it lawful for him from his injustice." Ibn al-'Arabi said: thus there are three views on the question. The first: he should not release him under any circumstances; this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. The second: he should release him; this was said by Muhammad ibn Sirin. The third: if it is property, he releases him, and if it is injustice, he does not release him; this is the view of Malik. The reasoning of the first is that one should not make lawful what Allah has forbidden, as that would amount to altering the ruling of Allah. The reasoning of the second is that it is his right, so he may waive it just as he may waive his blood and honour. The reasoning of the third, which Malik chose, is that when a man is unable to fulfil your right, it is kindness to him to release him; but if he is a wrongdoer, it is right not to leave him, lest the wrongdoers be emboldened (in some manuscripts: "and conceal themselves"; in others: "and seek counsel") and proceed in their ugly deeds. In Sahih Muslim is the lengthy hadith of Abu al-Yusr, in which he said to his debtor: "Come out to me, for I know where you are." So he came out, and he said: "What prevented you from hiding from me?" He said: "By Allah, I will tell you and not lie to you. I feared by Allah that I would tell you and lie, and that I would promise you and break it. You were a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and by Allah I was in hardship." He said: "I said: 'By Allah?'" He said: "By Allah." He said: "Then he brought a document and erased it, and said: 'If you find the means to pay, then pay; otherwise you are released...'" and he mentioned the hadith. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this applies to the living one from whom payment is hoped, for the sake of the soundness of his obligation and the hope of his finding a way out; so how about the dead one who has no means of release and no obligation remaining with him?

The tenth point: Some scholars said: whoever is wronged and has property taken from him, he has only the reward of what was withheld from him until his death; then the reward passes to his heirs, and so on to the last of them, because the property passes after him to the heir. Abu Ja'far al-Dawudi al-Maliki said: this is sound in reasoning, and according to this view, if the wrongdoer dies before the one he wronged and leaves nothing, or leaves what his heir does not know to be unjust, the claim of the wronged person does not transfer to the heirs of the wrongdoer, because nothing remains with the wrongdoer that his heirs of the wronged person could claim.

(Marginal note) The eleventh point: Allah's saying ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾ means: he bears harm patiently, and "forgives" means he leaves retaliation for the sake of Allah, the Exalted; this applies to one who is wronged by a Muslim. It is related that a man insulted another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, and the one insulted kept his anger in and perspired, and wiped the sweat; then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it, when the ignorant ones neglected it." In sum, pardon is recommended, though in some circumstances the matter may be reversed, so that refraining from pardon becomes recommended, as mentioned earlier; this is when it is necessary to restrain the increase of aggression and cut off the source of harm. There is a report from the Prophet ﷺ indicating this: that Zaynab reviled 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both, in his presence, and he kept forbidding her but she did not desist, so he said to 'A'ishah: "Go ahead and retaliate." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih in this meaning. It was also said: "patience" is restraint from sins and concealment of faults. ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast matters﴾ means: of the determinations of Allah which He commanded. It was also said: of the determinations of right conduct to which one is granted success.

Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, together with the three verses before it; one of the Ansar had reviled him, and he responded, then he refrained. These are the Madani verses of this surah. It was also said: these verses concern the polytheists, and this was at the beginning of Islam before the command to fight, then the verse of fighting abrogated them; this is the view of Ibn Zayd, and it has been mentioned earlier.

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And whoever takes revenge after being wronged﴾ refers to Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah, 'Ali and all the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with them. ﴿Those, there is no path against them﴾ refers to Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all. ﴿The path is only against those who wrong the people﴾ refers to 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, Abu Jahl and al-Aswad, and every polytheist who fought on the day of Badr. ﴿And they seek to cause corruption in the earth﴾ refers to by injustice and disbelief. ﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾ refers to a painful one. ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾ refers to Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and all the people of Badr, may Allah be pleased with them all. ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast matters﴾ refers to their accepting ransom and their patience over harm.

The first issue concerns His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny (al-baghy) afflicts them﴾, meaning when the polytheists' oppression afflicts them. As for one who persists in transgression and injustice, the better course is retaliation against him, based on the indication of the preceding verse. It has also been said: that is, when tyranny afflicts them, they support one another against it until they remove it from them and repel it. Ibn Bahr said this. It returns to the generality we have mentioned.

The third issue concerns His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. The scholars said: God made the believers two kinds. One kind pardons the wrongdoer, so He began by mentioning them in His saying, ﴿And when they are angry, they forgive﴾ [al-Shura: 37]. The other kind retaliates against their wrongdoer. Then He clarified the limit of retaliation with His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, so one retaliates against the one who wronged him without transgressing. Muqatil and Hisham ibn Hujayr said: This refers to the one who has been wounded taking retribution (qisas) from the one who wounded him, and not from anything else such as abuse or insult. This was also said by al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and Sufyan. Sufyan said: Ibn Shubrumah used to say: "There is no one in Makkah like Hisham." Al-Shafi'i interpreted this verse as meaning that a person may take from the property of one who betrayed him an amount equal to what that person betrayed him with, without his knowledge. He cited in support the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Hind, the wife of Abu Sufyan: "Take from his property what suffices you and your child." So he permitted her to take that without his permission. The discussion of this has already been fully covered in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 335]. Ibn Abi Najih said: It is to be understood as reciprocity in wounds, and if someone says "may God disgrace him" or "may God curse him," then he may say the same. But slander is not met with slander, nor lying with lying. Al-Suddi said: God only praised the one who defends himself against one who wronged him, without transgression, by not exceeding the measure of what was done to him, as the Arabs used to do. The recompense is called an "evil" because it corresponds to it: the first evil harmed in property or body, and this retaliation harms the other in the same way. All of this has been fully covered in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 335].

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever leaves retaliation and makes peace between himself and the wrongdoer through pardon, ﴿his reward is with God﴾, meaning God will reward him for that. Muqatil said: So pardon is among the righteous deeds. What is sufficient on this has already been covered in Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 207], and praise be to God. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz mentioned on the authority of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: "Which of you are the people of virtue?" Some people will stand up, and it will be said: "Go to Paradise." The angels will meet them and say: "Where to?" They will say: "To Paradise." They will say: "Before the reckoning?" They will say: "Yes." They will say: "Who are you?" They will say: "The people of virtue." They will say: "What was your virtue?" They will say: "When we were treated with ignorance, we showed forbearance, when we were wronged, we were patient, and when we were harmed, we pardoned." They will say: "Enter Paradise, how excellent is the reward of the workers." He mentioned the hadith. ﴿Surely He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the one who begins with injustice, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has also been said: He does not love one who exceeds the limit in retaliation and goes beyond the bound, as said by Ibn 'Isa.

The fifth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾. That is, if a Muslim defends himself against an unbeliever, there is no way to blame him; rather he is praised for that with respect to the unbeliever. And there is no blame if an oppressor [in one text: the wronged one defends himself; in another: an oppressor defends himself against a Muslim] against a Muslim. So retaliation against an unbeliever is obligatory, against a Muslim it is permissible, and pardon is recommended.

The sixth issue concerns His saying, ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, against such there is no way [of blame]﴾. This is evidence that one may exact that right by himself. This divides into three categories. The first: if it is retaliation for a bodily harm owed to a human being, there is no sin upon him if he exacts it without transgression and his right is established before the judges. However, the ruler should rebuke him for having taken the retaliation outside of legal process, because of the boldness it entails in shedding blood. If his right is not established before the judge, then there is no sin on him between himself and God, but outwardly he is to be claimed against and held accountable and punished for his act. The second category: it is a right of God the Exalted in which no human has a claim, such as the punishment for fornication or the amputation for theft. If this is not established before a judge, he is to be taken to account and punished for it. If it is established before a judge, one considers: if it is amputation for theft, the punishment is dropped because the limb to be amputated no longer exists, and no further right is owed for this, since discretionary punishment (ta'zir) is merely disciplinary. If it is flogging, the punishment is not dropped by his act, because he transgressed while the place of punishment remained, so he is subject to its ruling. The third category: it is a right concerning property. The owner may contend for his right until he reaches it, if he is one who knows of it. If he does not know of it, one considers: if he is able to reach it when claiming, he may not take it secretly. If he cannot reach it by claiming, because the one who owes it denies it and there is no evidence to support him, then regarding the permissibility of taking it secretly there are two opinions. One: it is permitted, which is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Two: it is forbidden, which is the view of Abu Hanifah.

The seventh issue concerns His saying, ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾. That is, by their transgression against them, according to the majority of scholars. Ibn Jurayj said: that is, they wrong them by polytheism which opposes their religion.

"And they seek to cause corruption in the earth without right." This means in lives and wealth, according to the majority. Muqatil said: their transgression is their doing of sins. Abu Malik said: it is what the disbelievers of Quraysh hoped, that a religion other than Islam would prevail in Makkah. On this basis, Ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated by jihad, and this applies to the polytheists specifically. Qatadah's view is that it is general, and the apparent meaning of the statement supports this. We have explained this, praise be to Allah.

The seventh point: Ibn al-'Arabi said: this verse corresponds to the earlier verse in Bara'ah, which is His saying ﴿There is no path [of blame] against the doers of good﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91]. Just as Allah negated the path against those who do good, so He affirmed it against those who wrong, and He completed the explanation of both categories.

The eighth point: Our scholars differed regarding a ruler who imposes a fixed sum on the people of a city, collecting it from them and having them pay it according to their wealth. Is it permissible for one who is able to escape this to do so, while in that case the rest of the people of the city are taken for the full amount imposed on them? It was said: no, and this is the view of Sahnun from our scholars. It was said: yes, he may do so if he is able to escape, and this is the view of Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Nasr al-Dawudi, then the Maliki. He said: what supports this is Malik's statement concerning the collector who takes a sheep from the flock of one of the partners when the flock as a whole does not reach the minimum: it is an injustice upon the one from whom it was taken, and he has no recourse against his partners for anything. He said: I do not adopt what is narrated from Sahnun, because injustice has no parallel, and no one is obliged to thrust himself into injustice for fear that the injustice will be multiplied upon others. Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿The path is only against those who wrong the people﴾.

The ninth point: The scholars differed regarding halalah (granting release/forgiveness of debt or wrong). Ibn al-Musayyib would not grant release to anyone regarding honour or property. Sulayman ibn Yasar and Muhammad ibn Sirin would grant release regarding both honour and property. Malik held that release is permitted regarding property but not regarding honour. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, when he was asked about the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, "I do not grant release to anyone," that he said: "That differs." I said to him: "O Abu 'Abd Allah, a man lends to another man and he perishes with no means of repayment?" He said: "I think he should release him, and that is better in my view, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 18]." It was said to him: "A man wrongs a man?" He said: "I do not think that. In my view it contradicts the first. The first: he should not release him under any circumstances; this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. The second: he should release him; this was said by Muhammad ibn Sirin. The third: if it is property, he releases him, and if it is injustice, he does not release him; this is the view of Malik. The reasoning of the first is that one should not make lawful what Allah has forbidden, as that would amount to altering the ruling of Allah. The reasoning of the second is that it is his right, so he may waive it just as he may waive his blood and honour. The reasoning of the third, which Malik chose, is that when a man is unable to fulfil your right, it is kindness to him to release him; but if he is a wrongdoer, it is right not to leave him, lest the wrongdoers be emboldened (in some manuscripts: "and conceal themselves"; in others: "and seek counsel") and proceed in their ugly deeds. In Sahih Muslim is the lengthy hadith of Abu al-Yusr, in which he said to his debtor: "Come out to me, for I know where you are." So he came out, and he said: "What prevented you from hiding from me?" He said: "By Allah, I will tell you and not lie to you. I feared by Allah that I would tell you and lie, and that I would promise you and break it. You were a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and by Allah I was in hardship." He said: "I said: 'By Allah?'" He said: "By Allah." He said: "Then he brought a document and erased it, and said: 'If you find the means to pay, then pay; otherwise you are released...'" and he mentioned the hadith. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this applies to the living one from whom payment is hoped, for the sake of the soundness of his obligation and the hope of his finding a way out; so how about the dead one who has no means of release and no obligation remaining with him?

The tenth point: Some scholars said: whoever is wronged and has property taken from him, he has only the reward of what was withheld from him until his death; then the reward passes to his heirs, and so on to the last of them, because the property passes after him to the heir. Abu Ja'far al-Dawudi al-Maliki said: this is sound in reasoning, and according to this view, if the wrongdoer dies before the one he wronged and leaves nothing, or leaves what his heir does not know to be unjust, the claim of the wronged person does not transfer to the heirs of the wrongdoer, because nothing remains with the wrongdoer that his heirs of the wronged person could claim.

(Marginal note) The eleventh point: Allah's saying ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾ means: he bears harm patiently, and "forgives" means he leaves retaliation for the sake of Allah, the Exalted; this applies to one who is wronged by a Muslim. It is related that a man insulted another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, and the one insulted kept his anger in and perspired, and wiped the sweat; then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it and grasped it, when the ignorant ones neglected it." In sum, pardon is recommended, though in some circumstances the matter may be reversed, so that refraining from pardon becomes recommended, as mentioned earlier; this is when it is necessary to restrain the increase of aggression and cut off the source of harm. There is a report from the Prophet ﷺ indicating this: that Zaynab reviled 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both, in his presence, and he kept forbidding her but she did not desist, so he said to 'A'ishah: "Go ahead and retaliate." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih in this meaning. It was also said: "patience" is restraint from sins and concealment of faults. ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast matters﴾ means: of the determinations of Allah which He commanded. It was also said: of the determinations of right conduct to which one is granted success.

Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, together with the three verses before it; one of the Ansar had reviled him, and he responded, then he refrained. These are the Madani verses of this surah. It was also said: these verses concern the polytheists, and this was at the beginning of Islam before the command to fight, then the verse of fighting abrogated them; this is the view of Ibn Zayd, and it has been mentioned earlier.

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And whoever takes revenge after being wronged﴾ refers to Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah, 'Ali and all the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with them. ﴿Those, there is no path against them﴾ refers to Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all. ﴿The path is only against those who wrong the people﴾ refers to 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, Abu Jahl and al-Aswad, and every polytheist who fought on the day of Badr. ﴿And they seek to cause corruption in the earth﴾ refers to by injustice and disbelief. ﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾ refers to a painful one. ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives﴾ refers to Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and all the people of Badr, may Allah be pleased with them all. ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast matters﴾ refers to their accepting ransom and their patience over harm.

There are eleven issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny (al-baghy) afflicts them﴾, meaning when the polytheists' oppression afflicts them. It is possible that one of them abrogates the other. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said in a similar vein: "They disliked that they should humiliate themselves, so that the wicked would become bold against them."

Likewise Ilkiya al-Tabari mentioned in his Ahkam: His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾, its apparent meaning indicates that retaliation in this place is better. Do you not see that He linked it to responding to God, the Glorified and Exalted, and establishing the prayer? There are eleven issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns His saying, ﴿And those who, when tyranny (al-baghy) afflicts them﴾, meaning when the polytheists' oppression afflicts them. He also said right after this verse: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, against such there is no way [of blame]﴾. This implies permission of retaliation, not a command to it. As for one who persists in transgression and injustice, the better course is retaliation against him, based on the indication of the preceding verse. It has also been said: that is, when tyranny afflicts them, they support one another against it until they remove it from them and repel it. Ibn Bahr said this. It returns to the generality we have mentioned.

The seventh point: Ibn al-'Arabi said: this verse corresponds to the earlier verse in Bara'ah, which is His saying ﴿There is no path [of blame] against the doers of good﴾ [At-Tawbah: 91]. The eighth point: Our scholars differed regarding a ruler who imposes a fixed sum on the people of a city, collecting it from them and having them pay it according to their wealth. Is it permissible for one who is able to escape this to do so, while in that case the rest of the people of the city are taken for the full amount imposed on them? It was said: no, and this is the view of Sahnun from our scholars. It was said: yes, he may do so if he is able to escape, and this is the view of Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Nasr al-Dawudi, then the Maliki. He said: what supports this is Malik's statement concerning the collector who takes a sheep from the flock of one of the partners when the flock as a whole does not reach the minimum: it is an injustice upon the one from whom it was taken, and he has no recourse against his partners for anything. He said: I do not adopt what is narrated from Sahnun, because injustice has no parallel, and no one is obliged to thrust himself into injustice for fear that the injustice will be multiplied upon others. So he came out, and he said: "What prevented you from hiding from me?" He said: "By Allah, I will tell you and not lie to you. I feared by Allah that I would tell you and lie, and that I would promise you and break it. You were a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and by Allah I was in hardship." He said: "I said: 'By Allah?'" He said: "By Allah." He said: "Then he brought a document and erased it, and said: 'If you find the means to pay, then pay; otherwise you are released...'" and he mentioned the hadith. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this applies to the living one from whom payment is hoped, for the sake of the soundness of his obligation and the hope of his finding a way out; so how about the dead one who has no means of release and no obligation remaining with him?

The tenth point: Some scholars said: whoever is wronged and has property taken from him, he has only the reward of what was withheld from him until his death; then the reward passes to his heirs, and so on to the last of them, because the property passes after him to the heir. Abu Ja'far al-Dawudi al-Maliki said: this is sound in reasoning, and according to this view, if the wrongdoer dies before the one he wronged and leaves nothing, or leaves what his heir does not know to be unjust, the claim of the wronged person does not transfer to the heirs of the wrongdoer, because nothing remains with the wrongdoer that his heirs of the wronged person could claim.
